Front: legal system
Back:
An operating set of
legal institutions, procedures and rules

Front: legal tradition
Back:
Deeply rooted, historically conditioned
attitudes about law, about what the law should be and should serve

Front: What does it mean to share the same legal tradition?
Back: sharing similar legal concepts, institutions, powers of the courts, processes

Front: legal culture
Back:
● The values, ideas and attitudes a society
has with respect to its laws

Front: what is legal culture affected by
Back: historical development and cultural norms

Front: what do we observe to understand a legal culture?
Back:
how disputes are resolved
how the law is perceived
dynamics in the courtroom ie how judges & lawyers behave
priorities (the law VS public policy VS the community)

Front: elements of a legal system (SSC)
Back:
● Structure

○ Institutional Bodies

○ E.g., Court system, judges, government
system

● Substance

○ What the rules themselves say

○ Rules on how institutions should behave

● Culture

Effect of social values, customs, opinions about
the law itself

Front: functions of legal system
Back:
● General function to distribute and maintain
an allocation of values that society feels to be right

○ Distributive justice

○ Commutative justice

● Settlement of disputes

● Social Control (Enforcement of rules of right
conduct)

○ Primary Social Control - Criminal Justice
(Arrest of Criminals)

○ Secondary Social Control
(Rehabilitation/Reformation, Deterrence)

● Social Engineering - Harvesting in demands
of society and making rules and values (Defines the “norms” of society)

● Recording Function - Administrative Reason

Symbolic Function - Punishment of crimes because
they offend solidarity of society

Front: views of the legal system
Back:
- Conventional
View – Law is certain predictable, free from subjectivity (old)
- Legal Realism View –
Law cannot be predicted wholly from structure and rule (current)

Front: Friedman’s Theory of the Legal System
Back:
● Legal Culture is not directly affected by
social change

● Legal Culture is:

○ Customs

○ Opinions about the law

○ Effect of Social Values

● Mechanistic Theory of the Legal System

○ Anything that goes in e.g. police complaint
(Input) should have a predictable
outcome (Output)

● Importance of rules and legal procedure

○ Distributes power among legal institutions;

○ Regulates the role of legal actors in the
process;

○ Creates/lessens the dependence of laymen on
lawyers;

○ Determines access to law and thus the
structure of power, and

Allows change only in valid and approved ways

Front: functions of the law
Back:
● Order

○ Law is an essential prerequisite of a
society that aspires to safeguard the well-being of its members

○ Surrendering of freedoms to create order

● Justice

○ Consists of treating equals equally and
“unequals” unequally, in proportion to their inequality

● Protection of Property

● Protection of Community’s General
Well-Being

Protection of Individual Rights

Front: How is law an allocative system?
Back:
- Legal decisions are by nature
economic, as they allocate scarce goods and services. The legal system is
a rationing system that reflects the distribution of power in society.

- The allocation takes into
account the following factors:

- Need: (prioritise large and low
income families)

- Merit (beauty, wisdom, virtue)

- Ascriptive/Status (Birth, Sex,
Religion, Income, etc.)

- Chance (Luck)

- Lottery (Equality of
Opportunity)

- Constitutional (Determines the
way decisions are made)

Front: factors of western legal tradition
Back:
- Distinction in Functions and Authority of
Legal Institutions
- Nature of Legal Doctrine as Academia
- Law being coherent with its Internal Logic
- The Formation of Legal Industry

Front: common law VS civil law origins
Back: English law vs Roman law

Front: common vs civil law sources of law
Back: court decisions VS civil code

Front: common vs civil attitude towards judicial decisions
Back: incrementalism (judicial precedents) vs principles in cases never binding

Front: common VS civil law: role of legislation
Back: statutes provide exceptions to an established line of cases, often adopted to amend the common law VS statutes are main source of law

Front: common vs civil law interpretation of legislation
Back: very restrictively vs broadly

Front: common vs civil: manner in which legislation is drafted
Back: very detailed statutes VS very general terms

Front: common VS civil law court structure
Back: one supreme & final court of appeal VS different matters have different final courts, no single court has jurisdiction over all these highest courts

Front: common vs civil law powers of the court
Back: injunction and contempt of court present VS no injunctions, no equivalent of contempt of court

Front: common vs civil law approach to problem solving
Back: more pragmatic, less theoretical VS less pragmatic, more theoretical

Front: common vs civil law premise
Back: remedial based VS rights based

Front: common vs civil law jury system
Back: present vs absent

Front: common vs civil law separate facts & law
Back: jury decides on facts, judge decides law VS no separation

Front: other examples of legal traditions
Back: religious laws, chinese law, customary law, mixed legal systems

Back:
supremacy of regular law over abitrary power
equality of all before the law
constitution being a consequence of the rights of individuals, and being enforced by the courts

Front: colonial legal traditions
Back:
● Dutch

○ Careful, non-interventionist forms of
colonisation

○ Dutch laws only applied to Europeans/people
with European statuses

● British

○ Introduced English common laws to their
territories, treating them as terra nullius (inhabited islands)

○ Straits settlements then adopted British
Indian Law for a period

● French

○ Introduced Code Napoleon

○ Highly sophisticated Chinese based laws in
Vietnam
French laws applied differently to different Vietnamese
territories
